FrMS88-de6041-d1e111.summary: Poses the seventeenth question: whether intuitive knowledge of the divine essence can be communicated to a wayfarer. Against: Moses was told 'No man shall see me and live'.
claims: Scripture seems to deny that a living person can see God.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e122.summary: Contrary: Jacob saw the Lord face to face.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e127.summary: States that one must first see what intuitive knowledge is.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e132.summary: Then the question itself. Reports the definition: intuitive knowledge is of a thing through itself.
claims: Reported definition: intuitive knowledge is of a thing through itself.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e140.summary: Abstractive knowledge is of a thing through a representative.
claims: Reported definition: abstractive knowledge is through a representative.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e145.summary: Objects: specifically different kinds of knowledge cannot share a constitutive difference; but, as said, abstractive cognition also terminates at the thing in itself, so this does not properly distinguish intuitive from abstractive.
claims: Terminating at the thing in itself is common to intuitive and abstractive cognition.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e156.summary: Reply: though both terminate at the thing in itself, in abstractive knowledge the thing does not cause or move it but the representative does, whereas intuitive knowledge terminates at and is caused by the thing itself.
claims: Intuitive cognition is caused by the thing itself; abstractive by a representative.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e167.summary: First objection: the soul understands itself abstractively, yet not through a representative but through its essence.
claims: Objection: the soul knows itself abstractively without a representative.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e174.summary: Second objection: many objects intuitively intelligible cannot cause, such as relations and prime matter, so knowledge of them terminates at but is not caused by them.
claims: Objection: relations and prime matter are intuited but cannot cause.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e185.summary: Third objection: whatever God can do through a secondary cause he can do immediately; he can cause intuitive knowledge through the object, so also without it, and it would terminate at the object without being caused by it.
claims: Objection: God could cause intuitive cognition without the object's causality.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e197.summary: Fourth objection: God sees his essence and creatures in it, not in themselves but in a representative, so not intuitively; and the blessed see the divine essence intuitively though it does not move them, since it is not a productive principle ad extra.
claims: Objection: God's knowledge of creatures and the blessed's vision are not caused by their objects.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e211.summary: Reply to the first: the soul knows itself neither intuitively nor abstractively but argumentatively, from an intuitively known object, namely its act of understanding.
claims: The soul knows itself argumentatively from its intuitively known acts.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e218.summary: Reply to the second: intuitive knowledge is that caused by the thing itself, or such as the thing would cause if it had causal power and could cause it.
claims: Intuitive cognition is what the object causes or would cause if it could.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e227.summary: Reply to the third: grants the major; God can supply the role of the cause but not of the terminus, since the act requires the terminating object's existence; or, as before, if God supplies the cause, he causes such knowledge as the thing would be apt to cause.
claims: God can supply the causal role of the object but not its terminating role.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e238.summary: Reply to the fourth: as said earlier, knowledge is specified by its first object; since God's knowledge of his essence is intuitive, it is called intuitive with respect to secondary objects like creatures; likewise for the blessed.
claims: Knowledge is specified by its first object.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e252.summary: Notes that intuitive knowledge concerns four contradictory extremes from which abstractive knowledge abstracts. First, actual existence: if a thing is known only as quiddity and not as actually existing, it is known abstractively.
claims: Intuitive cognition concerns actual existence; abstractive concerns only quiddity.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e265.summary: Second, presence: by common law intuitive knowledge concerns a present object, though God could perhaps make it otherwise.
claims: By common law intuitive cognition requires the object's presence.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e272.summary: Third, causation: by common law intuitive knowledge is caused by the thing at which it terminates.
claims: By common law intuitive cognition is caused by its object.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e277.summary: Fourth, motion: by common law the object must move the intellect. Turning to the second part of the question, says the answer varies according to different views of happiness.
claims: By common law the object moves the intellect in intuitive cognition.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e286.summary: Four opinions on happiness. Those placing it in the act of intellect must answer no: what is essentially beatitude cannot be in the soul without the soul being blessed, and vision of the divine essence would then be beatitude, making the wayfarer no longer a wayfarer.
claims: If beatitude is the intellect's act, intuitive vision cannot be given to a wayfarer.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e302.summary: Those placing happiness solely in the act of will must answer yes: of two essentially ordered and really distinct acts, the prior can exist without the posterior; the intuitive act of intellect is prior to the act of will, so it can be communicated without it, and what is communicated without beatitude does not remove one from the way.
claims: If beatitude is the will's act, the intellect's intuitive vision can be given to a wayfarer.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e325.summary: Those holding that beatitude is integrated from acts of intellect and will can also say yes: a whole is not posited by positing one integral part, so the intellectual act alone would not constitute beatitude.
claims: If beatitude is an integral whole of both acts, the intellect's act alone does not make one blessed.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e341.summary: Those holding beatitude to be a genus with the two acts as species must say no with the first view, since positing a species posits the genus. Then raises four difficulties, the first whether intuitive and abstractive differ in species: yes, since when a universal cause (the intellect) produces two essentially ordered effects through different particular causes (the thing itself, the representative), varying the particular cause varies the effect.
claims: If beatitude is a genus of intellectual and volitional acts, the intellect's vision would make one blessed.
Intuitive and abstractive cognition differ in species.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e372.summary: Second difficulty: whether they are essential differences of knowledge in general. No: of two essential differences dividing a genus, everything under the nobler is nobler than everything under the other, but abstractive knowledge of God is nobler than intuitive knowledge of whiteness.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive are not essential differences of knowledge in general.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e388.summary: Third difficulty: whether they are compossible in the same knower about the same object. Yes: angels know the same things in the Word (intuitively, even of the future) and in their proper genus (abstractively).
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition of the same object can coexist in one knower.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e399.summary: Fourth difficulty: whether the same knowledge can be both intuitive and abstractive. One might say yes with respect to different objects, but he proves no: the likeliest candidate would be God's and the blessed's knowledge of non-existents, yet it is intuitive only, since no abstractive knowledge knows accidents per accidens, while God and the blessed know the accidents of what they know.
claims: No single cognition is both intuitive and abstractive.
God's and the blessed's knowledge of creatures is intuitive because it reaches accidents.

FrMS88-de6041-d1e421.summary: Reply to the opening argument: 'no man shall see me and live' is understood of purely natural powers.
claims: Moses' text excludes vision of God by purely natural powers.

FrMS88-de6041.summary: The seventeenth question of the prologue asks whether intuitive knowledge of the divine essence can be communicated to a wayfarer. Meyronnes first defines intuitive cognition. Since abstractive cognition also terminates at the thing in itself, the difference is that intuitive cognition is caused by the thing itself (or is such as the thing would cause if it could), while abstractive is caused by a representative. He answers objections: the soul knows itself neither intuitively nor abstractively but argumentatively from its intuited act; God can supply the role of causing but not of terminating; and God's and the blessed's knowledge is intuitive throughout because knowledge is specified by its first object. Intuitive cognition concerns four contradictory extremes from which abstractive abstracts: actual existence, presence, causation by the object, and motion by the object (the latter three by common law). On the question itself, the answer depends on the theory of beatitude: if beatitude is the intellect's act, or a genus whose species are the acts of intellect and will, the answer is no, since intuitive vision would make the wayfarer blessed; if it is the act of will alone, or integrated from both acts, the answer is yes, since the prior intellectual act can exist without the posterior. Four further difficulties are settled: intuitive and abstractive cognition differ in species; they are not essential differences of knowledge in general (abstractive knowledge of God is nobler than intuitive knowledge of whiteness); they are compossible in the same knower of the same object (as angels' knowledge in the Word and in proper genus); and no single knowledge is both, God's and the blessed's being intuitive since they know accidents. Moses' 'no man shall see me and live' refers to purely natural powers.
claims: Intuitive cognition is caused by the object itself, or is such as the object would cause; abstractive is caused by a representative.
Cognition is specified by its first object, so divine knowledge is wholly intuitive.
Intuitive cognition concerns existence, presence, causation, and motion by the object.
Whether intuitive vision of God can be given to a wayfarer depends on whether beatitude lies in the intellect, the will, or both.
Intuitive and abstractive cognition differ in species but are not essential differences of knowledge in general.
Intuitive and abstractive cognition of the same object can coexist in one knower.
